From this, gold can be made just as easily as from other metals, unless it is deprived of its heat or its natural operation is not taken away from it. But if the power of a greater natural heat should reach that <term>quicksilver</term> <gloss>mercury</gloss> before it has reached its finished form—namely, the form of silver—so that it is reduced into a pure and red sulfur of Nature, then gold is formed from it more quickly than silver. It remains in that state perpetually, as the end toward which Nature tends in its laboring.

<term>Quicksilver</term> <gloss>mercury</gloss>, which we have just mentioned, is the mother of all metals because of its coldness and moisture. If it is pure and separated from all superfluity, then no more coarseness can be mixed with it, such that it would be reduced back into some <term>imperfect metal</term> <gloss>base metal such as lead or tin</gloss>. For Nature does not work backwards, nor is it a matter that looks toward any impure form, such as imperfect metals are. But sulfur is the father of all metals because of its heat and dryness. Following this distinction, let it be observed that quicksilver is described in the following chapter.

## CHAPTER II.

Therefore, there is in all metals a true Mercury and a right sulfur, in both imperfect and perfect metals alike. In the imperfect metals, these have merely been made contaminated and impure, and they lack perfect maturation. For these same reasons, they can be reduced to gold and silver: that is, the impurity with which they were defiled can be separated from the golden or silvery nature within them, and the form of gold or silver can be introduced to them. They are torn away from Nature when they are removed and dug out from the natural passages, minerals, and veins of the earth. Because of this, they can no longer undergo any operation within themselves as if they were still hidden beneath the earth. Nevertheless, as much as is within them, they desire to be perfected.

<summary>This page explains the alchemical maturation of metals, asserting that the balance of heat and the purity of sulfur and mercury determine whether gold or silver is formed. It argues that all metals contain the same essential essence and can be perfected if their impurities are removed.</summary>
